stories.headline: Australian Man Charged With Murder After 17-Year-Old Girl's Body Found in Suitcase in Thailand
stories.summary:
Thai police arrested Australian national Simon Peter Carman at Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi Airport in the early hours of Saturday after CCTV footage allegedly showed him entering a Pattaya condominium with 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla and later emerging alone carrying a large suitcase. The teenager's body was found stuffed in the bag near a railway track approximately 15 minutes after his airport arrest. Police said he was apprehended as he was allegedly preparing to flee the country.

Carman was charged with murder along with additional charges related to moving or concealing a body and taking a minor for sexual purposes. He denied all charges and claimed to have acted in self-defense. In a video recorded while in custody, he told the victim's family, "I feel bad for what happened to your daughter. It was out of my control," and added an admonishment for young women to "be careful."

The victim's father described himself as "deeply saddened" by his daughter's death, while her stepmother said she wanted Carman to "face the full consequences." Thai police in Pattaya said the girl had been reported missing Friday afternoon before the CCTV review led investigators to Carman.

The case has drawn significant international attention given the involvement of a foreign national, the victim's age, and the nature of the alleged crime in a major Thai tourist destination. Australian authorities have not yet issued a formal statement on the case.

stories.headline: More Than 50 House Members Warn South Korea's Proposed Platform Law Could Cost U.S. Economy $525 Billion
stories.summary:
More than 50 House lawmakers, led by Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., are pressing the Trump administration to confront South Korea over its proposed Online Platform Fairness Act, which the lawmakers say discriminates against American technology companies and tilts competitive advantages toward China-linked rivals. A model by the Competere Foundation estimates the legislation, if enacted, could result in $525 billion in lost U.S. economic activity over the next decade, including $123 billion in California, $48.7 billion in Texas, $33.9 billion in New York, and $27.4 billion in Washington state.

The bill, still pending in South Korea's National Assembly, would expand the powers of the Korea Fair Trade Commission to regulate transactions involving some American platform companies. It is backed by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, whose Democratic Party holds a substantial National Assembly majority following the 2024 impeachment and removal of conservative President Yoon Suk-yeol. Issa said South Korea's trade commission now "resembles the worst" of the Biden-era Federal Trade Commission under Lina Khan.

Some lawmakers have raised broader geopolitical concerns, with Issa warning that the current South Korean government's posture is "closely aligned with China" — an assertion that reflects growing unease in Washington over Seoul's orientation following the political transition. South Korea's government has not publicly responded to the congressional letter, and the legislation remains in an early stage.

Supporters of platform regulation argue that dominant U.S. tech firms have engaged in anticompetitive behavior that harms local businesses and consumers, a rationale similar to regulatory efforts underway in the European Union and other jurisdictions. Critics counter that singling out American companies amounts to economic nationalism that could damage a key alliance and benefit Chinese competitors who face fewer regulatory constraints.

stories.headline: Democratic Socialists Expand Footprint as Sen. Murphy Calls for Big-Tent Party; Mamdani Rejects Constitutional Change for Presidential Eligibility
stories.summary:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., argued Sunday that the Democratic Party should embrace democratic socialists as part of a broad coalition, saying "capitalism isn't working" for many Americans and that the party must confront concentrated corporate power. His comments came days after Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates won a series of New York City primary races and as DSA-aligned figures set their sights on state and congressional contests in Colorado, Wisconsin, and elsewhere.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the DSA-aligned democratic socialist who won the mayoral race last year, said Sunday he does not support amending the Constitution's requirement that presidents be natural-born U.S. citizens, even as his national profile has grown substantially. The 34-year-old, born in Uganda, told ABC News's "This Week" that the question of his own presidential eligibility under the current Constitution is moot as far as he is concerned.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries congratulated DSA-backed nominees following the New York primaries, a move that drew criticism from the Republican Jewish Coalition and prompted pushback from some New York City union leaders who said the party is moving too far left and out of touch with working-class voters. The intraparty tension signals a significant ideological debate within the Democratic Party ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Republicans have sought to use the DSA's rise as a political liability for mainstream Democrats, arguing that embracing democratic socialism will alienate moderate voters in competitive districts. Progressives counter that bold economic populism is precisely what a party in opposition needs to mobilize a disaffected base and draw contrast with Republican governance.

stories.headline: Three Firefighters Killed Battling Wildfire on Colorado-Utah Border
stories.summary:
Three firefighters were killed and at least two others injured Saturday while battling an out-of-control wildfire on the Colorado-Utah border, authorities confirmed. The firefighters, described as smokejumpers, died responding to a series of blazes that originated in eastern Utah's Grand County before spreading into Colorado, where multiple fires merged.

The deaths add to a severe Western fire season driven by a warm winter that produced below-normal snowpack across the region. The Cottonwood Fire in Utah had already been listed as the largest active wildfire in the United States, and multiple blazes continued to burn across the arid border region as of Saturday.

Firefighter fatalities in the line of duty are relatively rare and constitute a Tier 1 news event. The incident is being investigated by fire authorities to determine the precise circumstances of the deaths. No information on the victims' identities had been immediately released pending family notification.

stories.headline: Israel Cabinet Votes to Recognize Armenian Genocide, Straining Turkey Ties Further
stories.summary:
Israel's Cabinet voted unanimously on Sunday to designate the mass killing of Armenians by the Ottoman Empire during World War I as genocide, a historic policy shift that still requires approval by the Knesset to take full effect. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, who brought the measure to the government, called it a "moral and historical duty," noting that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders had previously described the events as genocide in personal statements but that no formal legislative recognition had ever occurred.

Historians estimate that up to 1.5 million Armenians were killed by Ottoman Turks around 1915 in what is widely regarded by scholars as the first genocide of the 20th century. Turkey fiercely contests the genocide designation, arguing the death toll has been inflated and that victims died in the context of broader wartime civil conflict. Turkey did not immediately respond to Sunday's vote.

The move reflects a sharp deterioration in Israeli-Turkish relations that has accelerated during the conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran. The two countries were once close strategic allies, but ties soured over the rise of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and have collapsed further in recent years. Israel now joins 32 other countries, including the United States, in formally recognizing the Armenian Genocide.

The timing carries additional diplomatic weight: Israel itself has faced repeated accusations from the United Nations and Turkey that its military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide, charges Israel rejects. Critics may note the irony of the timing, while supporters argue formal historical recognition has long been overdue regardless of current political circumstances.

stories.headline: Eleven Killed After Plane Carrying Skydivers Crashes Near Residential Area in Eastern France
stories.summary:
A civilian aircraft carrying skydivers crashed in Tomblaine, a town in the Meurthe-et-Moselle department of eastern France, killing all 11 people aboard, local authorities confirmed Saturday. The dead included the pilot, five parachute students, and five instructors. The plane had taken off from the nearby Nancy-Essey airfield when it went down.

The aircraft fell almost vertically near a housing estate on the edge of the airfield, according to Yves Seguy, the prefecture's top official, who told French broadcaster BFM that it was fortunate no bystanders were killed. The crash site is close to a shopping centre, and police urged the public to avoid the area.

French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot called the incident a 'terrible tragedy' and said he and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez were travelling to the scene. Local officials noted that approximately half of the victims were nurses, according to Thierry Pechey, president of the regional branch of the Order of Independent Nurses. Relatives of the victims were present at the airfield when the crash occurred.

stories.headline: Update: Venezuela Earthquake Survivors Describe Government Failure as Anger Grows in Caracas
stories.summary:
Weeks after dual earthquakes struck Venezuela, survivors in Caracas and the coastal town of La Guaira are expressing deepening frustration at what they describe as an inadequate government response. Displaced residents report sleeping outdoors, with no contact from authorities. 'If I was 30 and not 50, then maybe. But I don't know where to begin. And so far, no-one in authority has contacted us,' said former police officer Jan Carlos Roa Garcia, whose building was rendered uninhabitable.

In the hardest-hit areas, described by one BBC correspondent as 'apocalyptic,' more than 100 buildings have been flattened and rescue crews continue working around the clock hoping to find survivors. Interim President Delcy Rodriguez's tour of the Chacao neighborhood was met with public anger, with residents shouting that the government was 'campaigning in the middle of a tragedy.' Residents say it is ordinary Venezuelans — not the state — providing mutual aid.

International and Venezuelan rescue teams have continued to pull survivors from rubble, but hopes are fading and anger is growing, particularly in La Guaira. 'There are still people in there, we need machinery,' said one affected resident. The disaster is widely described by locals as the worst they have experienced in their lifetimes.

stories.headline: Budapest Holds First Pride March Since End of Orbán's 16-Year Rule
stories.summary:
Thousands of people marched through Budapest on Saturday for the Hungarian capital's first Pride celebration since the fall of Viktor Orbán's government, which had governed for 16 consecutive years. The march carries particular symbolic weight because Orbán's administration had passed both legislation and a constitutional amendment banning the event, drawing widespread condemnation from human rights organizations and European Union officials.

Orbán's nationalist-populist government fell more than a year ago, and the march represents one of the most visible public demonstrations of the shift in Hungary's political climate. The event drew participants from across the country and abroad, reflecting pent-up demand after years during which the event was legally prohibited.

The return of Budapest Pride is being closely watched across Central Europe as a signal of how quickly social and political norms can shift following the collapse of a long-entrenched government, and as EU institutions assess Hungary's trajectory after years of tension with Brussels over rule-of-law concerns.

stories.headline: Trump-Backed Candidates Sweep Alabama Runoffs; D.C. Mayor Race Too Close to Call
stories.summary:
President Trump's endorsement again proved decisive in Alabama Tuesday as Barry Moore won the Republican Senate primary runoff by nearly 14 points over Jared Hudson, defying pre-election polls that showed Hudson leading by wide margins. Moore attributed his victory directly to Trump's influence, saying older Alabama voters told him: "If the president endorsed you, we're with you." The Associated Press called the race before the state's most populous county, Jefferson, had reported most of its results.

Down-ballot, Trump-backed John Wahl won the Republican lieutenant governor primary, while Katherine Robertson secured the GOP attorney general nomination. Notably, Jay Mitchell — the state Supreme Court justice who authored a 2024 opinion declaring frozen embryos could be considered children, rattling the IVF industry — lost his Republican runoff for attorney general. Everett Wess, a former judge, won the Democratic Senate primary runoff but faces long odds in deep-red Alabama.

In Washington, D.C., the Democratic mayoral primary between democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George and moderate former councilman Kenyan R. McDuffie remained unresolved due to ranked-choice voting rules; a winner may not be declared for days or weeks. The D.C. race is among the most closely watched local contests of the cycle, testing whether progressive or moderate politics holds sway in the capital.

stories.headline: Update: European Heatwave Sets All-Time Records Across Central and Eastern Europe as Infrastructure Buckles
stories.summary:
The record-breaking heat wave that struck western Europe this week pushed into central and eastern Europe on Saturday, with Switzerland recording 38.8 degrees Celsius (101.8 F) in Basel and the Czech Republic logging its hottest day ever at 40.8 C (105.4 F) in the northern town of Doksany. Denmark's Meteorological Institute reported 37 C (98.6 F) north of Aarhus — the warmest temperature since records began in 1874. A new study released Saturday concluded the extreme heat would not have been possible without climate change.

Germany bore significant infrastructure damage: sections of the Autobahn burst from the heat and had to be closed, rail operator Deutsche Bahn advised against all nonessential train travel, and dozens of nursing home residents in Dormagen were evacuated after interior temperatures reached 35 C (95 F). One resident died overnight, though authorities had not confirmed heat as the cause. France banned alcohol sales in Paris as multiple eastern towns recorded their highest-ever temperatures.

This update reflects materially new record-setting temperatures and infrastructure failures documented Saturday, extending a crisis that has strained health systems across the continent. England set a new record for its hottest June day for the third consecutive day, with a provisional 37.3 C in Santon Downham, and more than 1,400 schools across England and Wales closed fully or partially due to the heat.

stories.headline: Uganda's Army Chief Orders Military Shutdown of Nation's Leading Independent Media Outlets
stories.summary:
Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda's army chief and son of President Yoweri Museveni, ordered the closure of the country's leading independent media outlets in the early hours of Sunday, deploying armed soldiers to surround the headquarters of the Nation Media Group in Kampala. Television stations NTV and Spark TV were taken off air, and the Daily Monitor newspaper reported staff were barred from entering or leaving the compound. The Nation Media Group is one of the most influential media organizations in East Africa.

Kainerugaba posted on X that he does not "believe in a free press" and that his father had given him "the power to shut down any media house I want to." He declared that NTV and the Daily Monitor "will not re-open without my permission" and warned that "ALL media in Uganda will follow the rules." The general has a history of inflammatory statements and is widely seen as being groomed to eventually succeed his 81-year-old father, who won a disputed seventh term in January.

Opposition and human rights groups condemned the crackdown as emblematic of a repressive regime. Supporters of Museveni's government maintain that his administration has brought stability and economic growth to Uganda. The closure marks one of the most direct acts of military press suppression in the country's recent history, echoing a 2013 raid on the Daily Monitor and a 2007 forced shutdown of NTV.

stories.headline: Alaska Judge Rules 'Copycat' Dan Sullivan Can Appear on Senate Primary Ballot Against Incumbent
stories.summary:
A Superior Court judge in Alaska ruled Friday that a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan — sharing the same name and party affiliation as incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan — is eligible to appear on the August primary ballot. Judge Thomas Matthews overturned a June 15 decision by the Division of Elections that had disqualified the challenger, finding that the exclusion was based on an unstated "good faith" criterion not grounded in the state constitution, Alaska law, or the division's own regulations. State attorneys are appealing the ruling, with Tuesday as the deadline for a final decision so ballots can be printed for the Aug. 18 primary.

The incumbent senator and the National Republican Senatorial Committee have sharply condemned the challenger's candidacy, arguing it is designed to confuse voters and benefit Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola, whom Sen. Sullivan faces as his main general-election opponent. The senator has accused the challenger of coordinating with Democrats and the Peltola campaign, allegations all parties have denied. Under Alaska's election system, the top four primary finishers advance to a ranked-choice November general election regardless of party.

The Alaska Senate race is considered one of roughly a half-dozen highly competitive Senate contests in 2026, with Democrats targeting the seat in their bid to recapture the majority. The presence of a same-name candidate in the primary raises questions about voter confusion and ballot integrity that could reverberate through the campaign season.
